executive_summary: SGD/JPY last closed at 123.47 on 2026-10-05. The pair is quoted in yen per Singapore dollar, so a rising quote means a stronger SGD. The price date is four sessions after the 2026-10-01 valuation date; the gap is disclosed, and every level in this report is anchored to that close. Over one month the pair is up 0.11%, which is essentially flat. It is down 1.78% over three months and 1.27% over six, both yen gains, and up 6.23% over a year. It sits at the 68th percentile of its 52-week closing range of 116.20-126.96. The dominant story is a collision between the two legs' policy paths. Singapore is growing far faster (GDP 5.9% vs 0.73%) and has higher core inflation (2.2% vs 1.7%), which pushes MAS towards tightening and holds back the BoJ. Against that, the BoJ holds the more under-priced hiking path: three decisions inside the window against an MAS that can only move its band slope. That path is steadily eroding SGD's thin +67bp T-bill carry. The bilateral view differs from both standalone dossiers. Each currency is Neutral tactically, and both are Bullish strategically by similar amounts, so the dossiers alone almost cancel. The pair verdict, scored without price data, is Bullish tactically (score +0.144, conviction 2) and Bearish strategically (score -0.114, conviction 2). Both scores sit within 0.05 of their thresholds, so these are leans, not high-conviction calls. The tactical call rests on liquidation of the +72.0K speculative yen long before the 2026-10-30 BoJ Outlook Report. The chart does not confirm it: spot is below all three daily moving averages and the highs have been falling since July. That argues for a small, tightly stopped position, not a re-score. The trades are sequenced. Tactically, buy at 123.20-123.50, the top of a four-touch support zone, with a stop at 122.35 and a target of 124.40, and close the position by 2026-10-29. Strategically, the exit from that long becomes the entry: sell at 124.40-125.05, targeting 120.80 by mid-January 2027, with a stop above 125.90.

market_context.valuation_assessment: On valuation the two legs are as far apart as any pair in the set. The BIS REER is 114.81 for SGD (75th percentile of its 2024-26 range, second-richest in G10+SGD) against 66.02 for JPY (about the 2nd percentile, 28.8 points below the next-cheapest currency). The SGD dossier's REER-relative proxy puts SGD/JPY fair value near 70.8, so SGD is 74% rich; the JPY dossier's PPP-style estimate puts it near 92, so the yen is 25% cheap. Both point the same way: on valuation the pair should fall over time. Neither is a timing signal. The yen has been cheap for years without reverting, and MAS management keeps SGD's richness in place. The current level prices SGD's productivity premium and appreciating band, and a yen that is still structurally a funding currency. It does not price a convergence in real exchange rates. Pass 1 treated valuation as a cap on confidence inside Factor 5 rather than a reason for a stance.

The narrative now centres on how quickly the BoJ follows up, measured against an MAS decision that is close to a coin flip.

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: Annualised carry. On the SGD dossier's 6M SGS T-bill proxy of 1.92%, against the BoJ's 1.25%, carry is +67bp to SGD (about 83 pips a year at 123.47). On 3M compounded SORA (Q2 average 1.06%) it is about -19bp, so even the sign depends on the basis. Carry-to-vol ratio is null by rule: no 3M implied vol exists for any SGD pair (for context only, carry against realised vol is 0.09 on 60-day and 0.13 on 20-day). Carry regime: marginal and shrinking. One ATR day (81 pips) roughly equals a full year of carry, so carry cannot drive flows in this cross. Each BoJ hike removes about 25bp: two hikes leave about +17bp, and three put the carry at roughly zero to negative. The 22bp rise in Singapore's 6M bill over two weeks came from US dollar funding pressure, not domestic policy, and it fades if the Fed stops. No listed forward or futures curve exists because SGD has no listed future; the indicative covered-interest-parity figures are money-market constructs, not a quoted funding differential. On the SORA basis SGD trades at a small forward premium (about +12 pips at six months, outright about 123.58).

tactical.bilateral_analysis: SGD has no policy rate. The bilateral short-rate gap therefore uses the SGD dossier's proxy, the 6-month SGS T-bill cut-off of 1.92% at the 24 September auction, against the BoJ call-rate target of 1.25% set on 2026-09-18. On that basis SGD earns about +67bp of carry over JPY, one of only three peers SGD out-yields. On 3-month compounded SORA (a 1.06% Q2 average) the sign flips to about -19bp, so the carry is thin and depends on which basis is used. The term structure already favours JPY. SGS 2y at 1.97% is only about 4bp above JGB 2y at 1.93%. SGS 10y at about 2.49% is now about 57bp BELOW the live JGB 10y of 3.05-3.07% (the payload's 2.94% JGB 10y is a monthly 2026-08-01 print and is not quoted as live). Two scheduled policy decisions fall inside four weeks. The BoJ decides on 2026-10-30 with an Outlook Report; OIS prices a hike at about 25-38%, against 40-45% in the JPY dossier. The MAS October statement is not on the gated meetings file (the SGD dossier expects late October, date unconfirmed); the survey prices a 45% chance of steepening, against 40% in the SGD dossier. The BoJ leg is the more under-priced of the two. Even so, a hold on 2026-10-30 is the base case and leaves the carry intact, so the tactical rates picture is offsetting rather than directional.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the direction of the differential matters more than its level, and it runs against SGD. The gated file has three BoJ decisions in the window: 2026-10-30 and 2027-01-22, both with Outlook Reports, and 2026-12-18. The JPY dossier's base case is two more 25bp hikes, which would take the BoJ to 1.75%. That would shrink SGD's T-bill carry from about +67bp to about +17bp, or to nothing if Singapore bill yields give back their quarter-end spike. MAS cannot respond through a rate. Its lever is the S$NEER slope, and the most it is expected to do is move from about 1.25% to 1.50%. That adds only about 0.15% of appreciation against the basket over six months, and nearly all survey respondents expect no change in January 2027. The curves already reflect this. JGB 10y now yields more than SGS. The JGB 2s10s curve, at about +112bp, is much steeper than Singapore's at about +52bp. The 2y gap has narrowed to about 4bp. The 22bp jump in Singapore's T-bill over two weeks came from US dollar funding pressure, not domestic policy. That support is borrowed from the Fed and fades if the Fed stops hiking. The result is that SGD's last carry advantage over JPY is eroding while the BoJ holds the more under-priced policy path.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The growth and inflation gap is the widest of any factor and clearly favours SGD. Singapore's Q2 GDP grew 5.9% y/y (1.4% q/q sa), against 0.73% y/y and 0.4% q/q for Japan, where private consumption added nothing and capex fell 0.9%. Inflation diverges in the direction that matters for policy. MAS core rose to 2.2% in August, in the upper half of its 1.5-2.5% range. Japanese core excluding fresh food eased to 1.7%, a seventh straight month below target. That combination strengthens MAS's tightening bias and weakens the case for the BoJ's next move. Recent surprises also favour Singapore. NODX rose 46.2% y/y against a 35% consensus. In Japan, August industrial production fell 1.7% m/m against a +1.4% forecast, retail sales missed, household spending fell 3.6% y/y, and the large-manufacturer Tankan missed at +24. Singapore's near-term releases are expected to stay firm: Q3 advance GDP (2026-10-W2), September NODX (2026-10-W3) and September CPI (2026-10-W4). Japan's 2026-10-06 wage print is the main JPY-positive data risk. The channel is relative policy expectations: strong Singapore data raise the odds of an MAS steepening, and soft Japanese demand holds down October BoJ odds.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the growth gap persists, but each side carries a risk that partly offsets the other. Singapore's boom is concentrated in AI electronics (electronics NODX +131.8% y/y). The MAS survey sees growth slowing to 3.1% in 2027, and retrenchments at a five-year high point to weakness outside AI. Japan's inflation picture is more two-sided than its 1.7% core suggests. The producer price index runs at 7.6% and electricity prices are held down by subsidies, so a subsidy roll-off could push core back above 2% and revive BoJ urgency. A 2.6% three-year-ahead inflation expectation in the Tankan and a 5.01% Shunto support that path. Both economies ride the same semiconductor cycle (Japanese electronic-component exports rose 52.3%), so an AI downturn would hit both, though Singapore depends on it more. On balance, Singapore's growth and core-inflation profile keeps MAS leaning towards tightening into Q1 2027, while weak Japanese demand limits how fast the BoJ can move. That is a moderate SGD-positive differential, held at lower confidence than tactically.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the starting point creates an asymmetry against the pair. With IG spreads near the floor of their post-crisis range and VIX at 16, changes are more likely to come as widening than tightening. JPY is the G10 currency that gains most from such a move, through two channels: repatriation by Japanese holders of about $3.5trn of foreign securities, and the unwinding of yen-funded carry. MAS's band management mutes SGD's response, so the pair's sensitivity to risk-off is dominated by the JPY leg. The specific tails are an AI-equity correction, which would hit Singapore's export engine and an STI that has gained 33.9% in a year, and a Hormuz re-escalation. A Hormuz shock hurts both importers, but over one to three months it has historically brought a yen safe-haven bid. The offset is that much of the yen carry-unwind fuel is already spent after the CFTC positioning flip, which reduces the likely size of the move but not its direction.

The JPY dossier's structural case is that long JGBs (10y 3.06%, 30y 4.15%) now yield more than currency-hedged Treasuries once 3-4% hedge costs are paid, reversing life-insurer outflows. Weekly data do not yet confirm it: Japanese investors bought 1,082.9bn yen of foreign bonds in the week to 2026-09-16. That flow mainly shows up in USD/JPY, since Japanese institutions hold little SGD, but it lifts the yen broadly and so lowers SGD/JPY. On the SGD side, the band ceiling rises about 0.6% over six months at a 1.25% slope, so today's crowding resolves through time, and wealth-management inflows are a steady bid. The yen short that was destroyed in September is slow to rebuild while JPY crosses keep losing money for carry holders. The 2027-03-31 Japanese fiscal year-end sits just beyond the three-month horizon. Net, mildly negative for the pair at low confidence.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The external-balance gap favours SGD on both stock and flow measures. Singapore's current account is about 16.6% of GDP (IMF 2026 projection; S$37.08bn in Q2), built on a goods surplus of S$70.39bn. Japan's 5.03%-of-GDP surplus rests on primary income that is mostly reinvested abroad. Its goods balance, the part that actually converts into FX flows, has been in deficit for four months (-1,105.6bn yen in August). Energy is the decisive difference. Both are net crude importers, but Japan imports about 99% of its oil and 94.2% of its crude from the Middle East, and its crude import bill is up 58.7% y/y. Singapore is partly hedged by its refining and trading hub and a S$14.33bn services surplus. Bilaterally, IMF DOTS shows Singapore running a goods deficit with Japan. Singapore reports $17.8bn of exports to Japan and $22.2bn of imports from it in 2024, a net -$4.5bn, which gives a modest structural JPY bid from Singapore importers. Japan's own figures ($19.8bn exports, $7.6bn imports) show the usual re-export reporting gap. The bilateral deficit is small next to Singapore's overall surplus, so the multilateral balance and the oil asymmetry dominate. Japan's current account on 2026-10-07 and Singapore's September NODX in 2026-10-W3 are the next prints.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months cumulative balance-of-payments flows favour SGD. With Brent around $98-101, up 53-57% y/y, and Hormuz shipping still below pre-war levels, Japan suffers a continuing transfer of real income through the terms of trade. That shows up as goods deficits even if oil prices stay flat. Singapore's AI-driven goods surplus is forecast to hold, with Enterprise Singapore raising its 2026 NODX forecast to 14-16%. The commodity rules point the same way: higher oil is strongly negative for JPY and only mildly negative for SGD, so energy shocks lift the pair. Two offsets keep confidence moderate. First, Japan's primary-income surplus and its roughly $3.3trn net international investment position put a floor under the external account, and both economies' export booms depend on the same semiconductor cycle. Second, valuation runs hard the other way: the BIS REER is 66.02 for JPY against 114.81 for SGD, the widest gap in the set, and the SGD dossier puts SGD about 74% rich against JPY on a REER-relative basis. That is a mean-reversion argument rather than a timing signal, and it is why confidence is not higher.

net_commodity_exposure.base_commodity_profile: SGD is a net crude importer with a large refining, bunkering and trading hub; the services surplus partly hedges energy volatility. Electronics and semiconductors dominate non-oil exports. Mildly negative to higher oil.
net_commodity_exposure.quote_commodity_profile: JPY imports about 99% of its oil (94.2% of crude from the Middle East) and most of its gas, with large exposure to Asian LNG spot prices. Strongly negative to higher oil and LNG.
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: 1. Oil up hits SGD mildly (-) under the import-dependence rule, cushioned by refining margins and trading activity. 2. Oil up hits JPY strongly (--) under the stated direction rules, and LNG (JKM) up also hits JPY strongly (--) while hitting SGD only mildly (-). 3. Netting -SGD against --JPY leaves a net positive for the base relative to the quote, so energy price rises push SGD/JPY higher and energy price falls push it lower. 4. Gold up is a CHF-type haven signal with no direct leg here, but risk-off episodes that lift gold usually also lift JPY, which is handled in Factor 3. 5. Semiconductor demand affects both exporters in the same direction and largely cancels. Bilateral investment context (pass 2, not scored): Singapore capital in Japan is substantial and long-dated; GIC describes itself as one of the largest foreign institutional investors in Japan, with a portfolio spanning office, retail, residential, hospitality, industrial and logistics. In the other direction, the top five source economies for Singapore's inward direct investment in 2022 were the United States, Japan, United Kingdom, Hong Kong and Mainland China. These are stock positions with long horizons, mostly hedged or sourced through USD, and they do not generate tactical SGD/JPY flow.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: Pair-positive. A 10% oil rise widens Japan's monthly goods deficit through a crude bill already up 58.7% y/y, while Singapore's import bill rises less and its trading hub partly benefits. The safe-haven risk is that an oil spike caused by Hormuz escalation also triggers a yen haven bid that outweighs the terms-of-trade effect.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: Pair-negative. Lower oil narrows Japan's goods deficit and removes the main external drag on JPY, while SGD gains less. A ceasefire-driven fall would also drain risk premia, which leaves the cross mostly to policy drivers.

strategic.score_interpretation: The net score of -0.114 is just through the -0.10 threshold, so the strategic stance is Bearish by rule. Five factors are JPY-positive (-0.307 combined), led by Policy & Rates at -0.134, and three are SGD-positive (+0.193), led by External Balance at +0.101. The margin is only 0.014. A single factor moving to Neutral (for example Factor 10) would push the score into the Neutral band, so the Bearish reading is marginal and should be treated as a lean rather than a conviction call. strategic.rationale: At strategic weights four blocks carry 62% of the weight: Policy and Rates (0.24), External Balance (0.18), Guidance (0.12) and Inflation and Growth (0.10). They split. Policy and Rates contributes -0.134, because the BoJ has three decisions on the gated file (2026-10-30, 2026-12-18, 2027-01-22) through which it can erase SGD's thin carry, while MAS can at most move its slope by 25bp. Guidance adds -0.062, because the BoJ's stated reaction function is under-priced by 15-25bp and MAS's is not. Against that, External Balance contributes +0.101 on Singapore's 16.6%-of-GDP surplus and Japan's oil-driven goods deficit, Inflation and Growth +0.054 and Fiscal +0.039 ahead of Japan's December FY2027 budget. Risk asymmetry (-0.038), institutional flows (-0.031) and dollar sensitivity (-0.042) tip the net to -0.114, Bearish by rule. The dossiers almost cancel: SGD +0.216 and JPY +0.250 strategically, a raw gap of about -0.03. The bilateral lens adds negative weight because SGD's strongest supports, its external surplus and MAS credibility, act mostly against the dollar and high-yielders, while JPY's main driver, BoJ normalisation, acts directly on this cross. What is priced is about two BoJ hikes over twelve months and a steady MAS slope. The edge is a BoJ path that is faster than priced, against an MAS with almost no room to surprise. The path of least resistance is a mild decline in the pair through the BoJ's forecast rounds, interrupted by Japan's December budget, which is the main yen-negative risk. Key dates are the 2026-10-30 and 2027-01-22 Outlook Reports, the 2026-12-18 BoJ decision, the 2026-12-09 FOMC, the December budget compilation and the MAS October and January statements (neither on the gated file). Conviction is 2: the score clears the threshold by only 0.014, the BIS REER gap (66.02 vs 114.81) is extreme but argues for mean reversion rather than timing, and an AI-cycle downturn or a BoJ stall would each overturn the call.
strategic.g10_relative_ranking: Strategically, short SGD/JPY ranks low among JPY longs. Among SGD crosses it is the one where SGD's strategic support is weakest, because JPY is the only peer with a hawkish, under-priced policy path that erodes SGD's small positive carry.

consensus_divergence.divergence_direction: Not determinable against a bank consensus for this pair, because none exists. Against a derived cross of the two USD-leg consensuses, the strategic view is in line in direction and the tactical view is more SGD-positive.
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Not quantifiable: no bank research consensus for SGD/JPY was found. The only pair-specific forecast pages located were extrapolation scripts and retail blogs, which are excluded by rule.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: No bank publishes a consensus for SGD/JPY in any free venue, so bank_consensus_forecast is null rather than filled from extrapolation sites such as LongForecast, 30rates, WalletInvestor or Traders Union, which would be a category error. An indirect reading is possible from the two dossiers' USD-leg consensuses. The aggregated institutional USD/JPY forecast in the JPY dossier implies about 3.6% yen appreciation over six months, while the MAS survey's end-2026 USD/SGD median is essentially flat. Together these imply a yen-favourable drift in the cross, the same direction as our strategic Bearish lean. Our tactical Bullish call departs from that implied path because we weight the +72.0K speculative yen long, and the near-term liquidation risk it carries, more heavily than the USD/JPY consensus does. That consensus expects the yen move to begin at once. This is a derived cross, not a bank consensus, and it is not reported as one. Pass-2 addendum: an indirect compilation of early-2026 USD-leg forecasts (Credit Agricole, DBS, ING, Westpac around 116-117; MUFG and DBS skewed to 112-114 by year-end) has been badly wrong on level, with spot about 650 pips higher, but is informative on direction: the sell-side cross view has been for a lower SGD/JPY all year. UBS projects USD/SGD in a sideways 1.25-1.31 range through 2026, so the cross inherits whatever the yen does. Before the September meeting, per MUFG, short-term rates markets were pricing slightly less than 3 more BoJ hikes to 1.9% by July 2027, a steeper path than the meeting-by-meeting OIS odds, which is a caveat to the claim that the BoJ path is under-priced. The strategic view lines up with the implied consensus direction; the tactical view is a deliberate contrarian deviation resting on positioning, with a small payoff and risk bounded by the 122.35 stop.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: Tactically, the cross benefits from yen-long liquidation into a BoJ hold. Strategically, it captures BoJ normalisation that is faster than priced, while SGD's carry cushion is too thin to offset it.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: Tactically, a BoJ hike on 2026-10-30 against 25-38% pricing would invert the call within days. Strategically, a BoJ stall at 1.25% combined with a December fiscal disappointment would leave SGD's growth and external-surplus advantages in control and lift the pair.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The horizons diverge because they are driven by different mechanisms on different clocks. Over four weeks, the stretched speculative yen long, the gap in growth and core inflation, and Japan's oil-driven goods deficit dominate, while the rates factor is Neutral because both central banks face near coin-flip decisions and a BoJ hold is the base case. Over one to three months, three BoJ decisions (two with Outlook Reports) let the under-priced policy path erode SGD's thin carry, the speculative long normalises, and the JPY leg's higher sensitivity to risk-off and to the dollar comes into play. Both stance scores sit within 0.05 of their thresholds, so the divergence is real but low-conviction on both sides.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: The BoJ Monetary Policy Meeting with Outlook Report on 2026-10-30, at the end of the tactical window. A hike, or a hawkish CPI-path revision, brings the strategic view forward; a hold with an unchanged path extends the tactical one. The MAS October statement, not on the gated file and unconfirmed for late October, is a secondary checkpoint.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: The two views can coexist if sequenced: the tactical bias applies only up to the 2026-10-30 BoJ decision, and the strategic lean takes over after it. Tactical long: buy 123.20-123.50, stop 122.35, target 124.40, flat by the 2026-10-29 close. catalysts.event: Japanese PM Takaichi parliamentary policy address
catalysts.rationale: The address sets out an expansionary fiscal programme from an administration widely assumed to prefer monetary accommodation, a standing yen-negative. A Nikkei preview on 2026-09-30 pulled JGB yields down 2.5-4bp, showing that reassurance lowers yields and weakens the yen-positive rate channel. Singapore has no offsetting event, so the impact runs through JPY alone and lifts the cross.

Wage growth is the BoJ's key test of whether inflation is sustainable. The prior overall wage print of +4.7% beat a 3.9% forecast. A second beat would raise the odds of an October hike, currently priced at only 25-38%, and strengthen JPY against an SGD that has no scheduled data that day, pushing SGD/JPY lower.

The test is whether Japan's primary-income surplus keeps outrunning a goods deficit that has lasted four months, at -1,105.6bn yen in August with crude imports up 58.7%. A goods-led deterioration confirms the oil asymmetry behind Factor 5 and supports the tactical long. Singapore's surplus has no equivalent release in the window.

catalysts.event: Singapore Q3 2026 advance GDP (MTI) (source date in week format 2026-10-W2, approximated to week start; not on the gated file)
catalysts.rationale: The MAS survey expects 4.6% y/y, and the SGD dossier sees 5% or more on NODX and PMI strength. Against Japan's 0.73% y/y, a strong print widens the growth gap and raises the odds of an MAS slope steepening shortly before the BoJ meeting, supporting the cross through relative policy expectations. Date in week format; not on the gated file.

catalysts.event: Singapore NODX (September) (source date in week format 2026-10-W3, approximated to week start)
catalysts.rationale: August NODX rose 46.2% y/y on AI electronics. A print of 25-40% keeps Singapore's goods surplus, the FX-generating part of its external balance, growing while Japan's goods account stays in deficit. A print below 15% would be the first sign that the shared semiconductor cycle is rolling over, which hits SGD harder. Date in week format.

catalysts.event: Singapore CPI and MAS core inflation (September) (source date in week format 2026-10-W4, approximated to week start; not on the gated file)
catalysts.rationale: MAS core was 2.2% in August, against Japanese core at 1.7%. A print of 2.3% or more would put Singapore core above the midpoint of MAS's range and strengthen the tightening case. That widens the policy-relevant inflation gap that drives the cross's Factor 2 contribution. Date in week format; not on the gated file.

catalysts.event: MAS October Monetary Policy Statement (NOT on the gated meetings file; late-October timing per the SGD dossier, unconfirmed; source date 2026-10-W4 approximated to week start)
catalysts.rationale: The gated decisions file has no MAS schedule, so this date is the SGD dossier's estimate and is not firm. The survey prices a 45% chance of the slope rising from about 1.25% to 1.50%; even a hold keeps the band appreciating against a basket that includes JPY. Its order relative to the 2026-10-30 BoJ decision cannot be fixed, and that order affects which bank sets the tone for the cross.

A further Fed hike would lift the dollar against both legs. Because the yen's dollar sensitivity is several times SGD's, it would normally lift SGD/JPY, though September showed that link can break. A signal that the Fed is pausing would release more yen than SGD upside and weigh on the cross. The decision lands two days before the BoJ and shapes the US-Japan front end going into it.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting with Outlook Report
catalysts.rationale: This is the single most important event for the pair and the inflection between the tactical and strategic views. OIS prices about 25-38% for a hike against 40-45% in the JPY dossier, and the Summary of Opinions shows a hawkish majority. A hike or an upgraded CPI path would cut SGD's carry, trigger nothing on the SGD side and pull the cross lower. A dovish hold would force yen-long liquidation and lift it.

catalysts.event: Japan national CPI (October) (source date in week format 2026-11-W3, approximated to week start; not on the gated file)
catalysts.rationale: Japanese core has been below 2% for seven months, but it sits beneath a 7.6% producer price index and a subsidy-suppressed electricity component. A sign that costs are starting to pass through would revive BoJ urgency and weigh on the cross. A further fall towards 1.4% would undercut BoJ normalisation and support SGD's carry. Date in week format; not on the gated file.

catalysts.rationale: Fitch has said it will scrutinise the budget for fiscal discipline under an expansionary administration. With debt near 260% of GDP and a 222bp JGB 2s30s spread, a disappointing budget would make rising yields read as sovereign risk rather than normalisation. That turns the rate channel yen-negative and lifts the cross against AAA-rated Singapore. Date in week format.

If October brings a hold with a hawkish forecast revision, December becomes the focal point and pricing should move up, compressing SGD's remaining carry advantage. MAS has no decision then, so the move falls entirely on the yen leg.

MAS's January statement is expected to be a non-event (and is not on the gated file), so this meeting sets the cross's strategic direction.

signposts.indicator: Core inflation gap: MAS core minus Japan core ex fresh food

signposts.bilateral_importance: The two banks react to inflation through different instruments (slope versus rate), and the gap decides whose instrument moves first in the October-January window.
